issues.description: Regex /\dm?s/i admits false positives that aren't time tokens.
issues.detail: The pattern matches any digit followed by 's' or 'ms' anywhere in the string, so values like '1solid' or '5something' or identifiers containing such substrings pass the gate. That is harmless for correctness here (the parser still rejects non-time values), but the comment/name HAS_TIME overstates what the predicate proves. A literate-programming-grade name would be MIGHT_CONTAIN_TIME, or the regex should anchor on word boundaries: /\d(?:ms|s)\b/i.

issues.description: Missing literate comment explaining why the fast-path regex is sound.
issues.detail: The optimization rests on an invariant: any declaration whose value contains a time token must contain a digit immediately followed by 's' or 'ms'. That invariant is not stated in code. A one-line comment ('cheap pre-filter; valueParser is the authority') would let a future reader confirm the regex is a conservative over-approximation of valueParser's time detection.

issues.description: No measurement included to justify the 'performance' claim.
issues.detail: The changeset asserts a performance fix but the PR carries no benchmark, profile output, or before/after numbers. The change is plausibly a win (avoids valueParser on every decl), yet the discipline is: measure, then optimize. A one-line benchmark result against issue #6869's reproducer would convert this from intuition to evidence.

review.summary: The change is a sensible cheap-predicate fast path in front of an expensive value parser — exactly the 3% optimization Knuth would endorse, provided it is measured. The asymptotic shape is unchanged; the constant factor improves because the common case (declarations with no time token) skips both vendor.unprefixed and valueParser. My concerns are literate, not algorithmic: the regex name overstates what it proves, there is no comment explaining the soundness invariant, and the 'performance' claim is unaccompanied by numbers. Verdict: RIGOROUS in shape, NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT in presentation.
